medications.monitoring: Serum zinc levels (though not always reliable). Monitor clinically for deficiency signs: poor wound healing, taste changes, hair loss, skin lesions.
medications.post_resection_considerations: Chronic diarrhea from any cause (including post-resection) increases zinc loss. Monitor and supplement proactively.
medications.special_notes: Long-term high-dose zinc depletes COPPER — must co-supplement copper. Zinc competes with iron for absorption — take at different times.

forms.magnesium_glycinate: PREFERRED for Crohn's/IBD patients. Well-absorbed (chelated form). Least likely to cause diarrhea. Gentle on the stomach. Also has calming/relaxation benefits.
forms.magnesium_citrate: Good bioavailability but DRAWS WATER into the bowel — can worsen diarrhea. Acts as a mild laxative. Avoid if you have active diarrhea.
forms.magnesium_oxide: Cheapest but WORST absorbed (only ~4% bioavailability). Also causes significant diarrhea. NOT recommended for Crohn's patients.
forms.magnesium_malate: Good absorption. May help with energy and muscle pain.
forms.magnesium_threonate: Crosses blood-brain barrier. Good for cognitive function but expensive.

medications.best_form_for_crohns: Magnesium GLYCINATE — best absorbed with least diarrhea risk. Critical for IBD patients who already have loose stools.

dosing.notes: Divide doses to improve absorption and reduce GI side effects

medications.crohns_relevance: Deficiency common due to chronic diarrhea, malabsorption, and certain medications (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, PPIs). Symptoms: muscle cramps, fatigue, weakness, irritability, abnormal heart rhythms.
medications.monitoring: Serum magnesium (though levels can be normal despite tissue depletion). RBC magnesium is a better marker but less commonly available.
medications.post_resection_considerations: Most magnesium is absorbed in the small intestine, including the ileum. Post-resection patients are at high risk for depletion, especially with ongoing diarrhea. Glycinate form is essential — oxide and citrate will worsen diarrhea.
medications.special_notes: AVOID magnesium oxide and magnesium citrate if you have diarrhea — they make it worse. Glycinate is the clear winner for Crohn's patients.

forms.folic_acid: Synthetic form. Most studied and widely available. Must be converted by the body to active methylfolate. ~40% of people have MTHFR gene variants that reduce this conversion.
forms.methylfolate_5_MTHF: Active form — no conversion needed. Better for patients with MTHFR variants. More bioavailable. More expensive.
forms.folinic_acid_leucovorin: Another active form. Used medically to 'rescue' from methotrexate toxicity.

medications.crohns_relevance: Depleted by: sulfasalazine (strong folate antagonist), methotrexate (folate antagonist), proximal small bowel disease/resection (folate absorbed in jejunum), and chronic inflammation.

dosing.on_methotrexate: 1-5mg folic acid daily — take every day EXCEPT the day you take methotrexate
dosing.methylfolate: 400-800mcg L-methylfolate daily (especially if MTHFR variant suspected)

medications.monitoring: Serum folate and RBC folate levels. Homocysteine (elevated in folate deficiency).
medications.post_resection_considerations: Folate is absorbed in the jejunum (upper small intestine), not the ileum. Ileal resection alone typically does NOT impair folate absorption. However, patients with extensive proximal small bowel disease or resection may be affected.
medications.special_notes: MANDATORY supplementation with sulfasalazine and methotrexate. Consider methylfolate if you know you have MTHFR variants or if standard folic acid doesn't correct your levels.

VSL_3_now_Visbiome.evidence: Some evidence for reducing inflammation after ileocecal resection (reduced inflammatory cytokines). Better evidence for UC pouchitis than for Crohn's. NOT proven for Crohn's maintenance of remission.

Saccharomyces_boulardii.evidence: Variable results. Some studies show benefit in combination with standard therapy for Crohn's. A yeast, not a bacterium — not killed by antibiotics. USE WITH CAUTION in immunocompromised patients (fungemia risk).

Lactobacillus_rhamnosus_GG.evidence: Mixed results for Crohn's. Better evidence for preventing antibiotic-associated diarrhea.

medications.overall_evidence_for_crohns: WEAK. A 2025 systematic review concluded there is NO proven role for probiotics in maintaining remission in Crohn's disease. Evidence is stronger for UC pouchitis (VSL#3) and antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Probiotics may have a role as adjunctive therapy but should NOT replace proven medications.
safety_concerns: Immunocompromised patients: risk of probiotic-related sepsis/fungemia (especially S. boulardii in severely immunosuppressed patients)
Quality control: supplement industry is poorly regulated; CFU counts may not match labels
Do NOT take live probiotics through central venous catheters
medications.post_resection_considerations: Some evidence that VSL#3 may reduce inflammatory markers post-ileocecal resection, but this has not translated into proven clinical benefit. May help with post-resection diarrhea subjectively. Use as adjunct, not replacement for proven therapies.
medications.special_notes: Despite widespread use, evidence for probiotics in Crohn's is disappointing. If you choose to use them, VSL#3/Visbiome and S. boulardii have the most (albeit limited) evidence. Discuss with your GI, especially if immunosuppressed.

medications.crohns_relevance: Anti-inflammatory properties. One early study showed 59% fish oil group in remission at 1 year vs. 26% placebo. However, two subsequent large, high-quality trials (EPIC-1 and EPIC-2) showed omega-3 fatty acids are probably INEFFECTIVE for maintenance of remission in Crohn's.

dosing.notes: Enteric-coated capsules may reduce fishy burps and GI side effects

medications.evidence_summary: Overall INSUFFICIENT evidence to recommend omega-3 for Crohn's disease maintenance. May have general health benefits but should not be relied upon for IBD management.
medications.post_resection_considerations: Fat malabsorption post-resection may reduce absorption of fish oil. If significant steatorrhea, may not absorb well. Consider algal-derived omega-3 or pharmaceutical-grade formulations.
medications.special_notes: Not harmful but probably not effective for Crohn's disease specifically. If using, choose high-quality, third-party tested brands to avoid contaminants.

medications.crohns_relevance: Glutamine is the primary fuel source for intestinal epithelial cells. Theoretical benefit for gut barrier repair ('leaky gut'). However, clinical evidence is DISAPPOINTING.
medications.evidence_summary: A Cochrane review and multiple systematic reviews conclude there is INSUFFICIENT evidence for glutamine in active Crohn's disease. No significant improvement in intestinal permeability or clinical remission in controlled trials. Subgroup analysis suggests doses >30g/day MAY have some effect on permeability, but this is not clinically proven.

dosing.notes: Evidence does not support routine use

medications.side_effects: Generally well-tolerated. Bloating, gas. At very high doses: potential for ammonia buildup in patients with liver disease.
medications.post_resection_considerations: Theoretical benefit for gut barrier repair post-surgery, but no clinical evidence supports this in Crohn's patients.
medications.special_notes: NOT recommended as a Crohn's treatment. If you choose to try it, it's unlikely to cause harm but evidence of benefit is lacking.

medications.crohns_relevance: Anti-inflammatory compound from turmeric. Reduces levels of inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IL-12). Multiple small studies show promising results but larger trials are needed.
medications.evidence_summary: Small studies show: 55% decrease in CDAI in 5 Crohn's patients over 2 months; Theracurmin formulation reduced CDAI from 211 to 149 (vs. 211 to 203 placebo, p=0.035). Anti-inflammatory mechanism is well-established. HOWEVER: curcumin has VERY poor bioavailability — most is not absorbed from the gut. Special formulations (Theracurmin, BCM-95, piperine/bioperine-enhanced) improve absorption.

dosing.studied_ranges: 360mg three times daily to 3g twice daily
dosing.enhanced_forms: Theracurmin 360mg/day, or curcumin with piperine (BioPerine) 500-2000mg daily
dosing.notes: Must use enhanced-absorption formulations for any meaningful blood levels

medications.drug_interactions: May interact with blood thinners (warfarin), blood sugar medications, and drugs metabolized by CYP enzymes. Discuss with pharmacist.
medications.post_resection_considerations: Poor absorption is made worse by reduced intestinal surface area. Enhanced-absorption formulations are even more important post-resection.
medications.special_notes: Promising but unproven for Crohn's. Use as adjunctive (alongside proven therapies), NOT as a replacement. Variable formulations make dosing recommendations difficult. If using, choose bioavailability-enhanced forms.

categories.name: Newest/Pipeline Medications (2025-2026)
categories.description: Recently approved and investigational therapies for Crohn's disease.

approved_2025.significance: First biologic in 15+ years to have 2-year Phase 3 data at time of approval. IL-23p19 inhibitor. 53% clinical remission at 1 year.
First IL-23 inhibitor with fully subcutaneous dosing option (no IV needed). GRAVITI and ASTRO trial data.

approved_2025.indication: Updated label for moderate to severe Crohn's disease

approved_2025.significance: Lower cost option for natalizumab therapy.
7+ biosimilars launched, dramatically reducing ustekinumab costs. Several have interchangeability designations.

pipeline_investigational.notes: Already approved for UC. Crohn's results pending. Caution after ozanimod Crohn's trial failure.

pipeline_investigational.status: Showed safety/tolerability over 12 weeks for ileal stricturing
pipeline_investigational.notes: Novel target — specifically for stricturing Crohn's disease. First-in-class for fibrosis/stricture treatment.
Deliberate combinations (e.g., IL-23 inhibitor + JAK inhibitor for induction) being studied for patients hitting therapeutic ceiling. 'Induction blasting' with JAKs is a new strategic concept.

drug_interaction_warnings.description: Allopurinol dramatically increases thiopurine levels by blocking metabolism. If intentionally combined (to optimize metabolites), azathioprine dose must be reduced by 75%. Fatal bone marrow suppression has occurred when combined at full doses.
NEVER combine. Dramatically increases risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) and serious infections.
Do not combine two biologics unless specifically directed by a specialist in a clinical trial setting. Profound immunosuppression risk.
Combination significantly increases risk of Achilles tendon rupture. Use with extreme caution, especially in patients >60.
NSAIDs reduce renal clearance of methotrexate, potentially causing toxic accumulation. Avoid combination.
Both are folate antagonists. Combination can cause severe bone marrow suppression. Avoid if possible.
Disulfiram-like reaction: severe nausea, vomiting, flushing, cramping. No alcohol for 3 days after stopping metronidazole.

Cholestyramine binds drugs in the gut. Take ALL other oral medications at least 1 hour BEFORE or 4-6 hours AFTER cholestyramine. This includes levothyroxine, warfarin, mesalamine, oral contraceptives, and vitamins.
Increase JAK inhibitor levels. Upadacitinib dose must be reduced when combined.

Do NOT give live vaccines to patients on immunosuppressants (thiopurines, methotrexate, biologics, JAK inhibitors). Live vaccines include: MMR, varicella, zoster (Zostavax — NOT Shingrix which is inactivated), yellow fever, oral polio, BCG, live influenza nasal spray.
These minerals chelate ciprofloxacin, dramatically reducing its absorption. Separate by at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after.
Sulfasalazine depletes folate. Not a dangerous interaction but requires mandatory folate supplementation (1-2mg daily).

medications_to_AVOID_with_crohns.drug: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin in anti-inflammatory doses)
medications_to_AVOID_with_crohns.reason: Can trigger Crohn's flares, cause small bowel ulceration, and increase emergency hospitalizations. ACG recommends avoidance. Use acetaminophen (Tylenol) for pain instead. COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) may be safer but use cautiously.
medications_to_AVOID_with_crohns.alternative: Acetaminophen for pain. Celecoxib (Celebrex) with GI approval if needed.

medications_to_AVOID_with_crohns.reason: Unnecessary antibiotics can disrupt gut microbiome and trigger Crohn's flares. Only use antibiotics when specifically indicated.
medications_to_AVOID_with_crohns.alternative: Use antibiotics only for documented infections, perianal disease, or SIBO.

medications_to_AVOID_with_crohns.reason: Some reports of IBD onset/flare, though causal link is debated. Use with caution and GI awareness.
medications_to_AVOID_with_crohns.alternative: Discuss dermatologic alternatives with both dermatologist and GI.

medications_to_AVOID_with_crohns.reason: Contraindicated while on immunosuppressive therapy. Can cause active infection from the vaccine strain.
medications_to_AVOID_with_crohns.alternative: Get all live vaccines BEFORE starting immunosuppressive therapy. Use inactivated alternatives when available (e.g., Shingrix instead of Zostavax).

take_with_food: Iron (with vitamin C for better absorption, though empty stomach is also OK)
take_on_empty_stomach: Asacol HD (mesalamine — 1hr before or 2hr after meals)
